title: FIRE (Financial Independence, Retire Early)
body:
O.P.
Hi all,
I had a look for a thread around FIRE and didn't find one.
I wanted to start a thread where Aussies can openly talk about it, as I don't know many people in person that are interested in it.
FIRE (Financial Independence, Retire Early) is essentially a concept around frugal living, and re-organising priorities with an emphasis on delayed gratification. The goal being to reach a point in your life where you have sufficient income producing assets to not have to rely on work to make ends meet.
I've only recently started looking in to it, but I'm keen to see if anyone has walked the path and has tips or insight, or just wants to chat about any aspect of FIRE!
Cheers

[User #413056480 postskivexForum Regular] Yep, we are on the FIRE path. I first came across MMM back in 2014-2015, however it didn't click until January 2017. At that time we put our ten year plan into action, deciding to FIRE around December 2026, which corresponds with our youngest completing high school.
We joke that we are now on the eight and a half year plan ... by the end of the year we'll be on the eight year plan and so on.
We are doing it the boring way – Vanguard funds – as typically recommended.
Conservative projections indicate we'll meet our dollar target – perhaps sooner if the universe/market smiles on us, however even so, we won't pull the plug until the end of 2026.
[User #893501059 postsengagedWhirlpool Enthusiast] Cory the Creator writes...
FIRE (Financial Independence, Retire Early) is essentially a concept around frugal living, and re-organising priorities with an emphasis on delayed gratification. The goal being to reach a point in your life where you have sufficient income producing assets to not have to rely on work to make ends meet.
I am interested in hearing peoples reasons for doing this in the first place. From a very high-level it looks like people are working hard in jobs they don't particularly like – living like monks – and saving like mad. Then at some point they will be able to stop working – live off their assets – and then what? I assume they will probably still be living like monks as that is all they know now – and trying to find a vocation that is meaningful.
Wouldn't it be better to look at this the other way – find that vocation that is meaningful to you – then make it work with the income it produces.

find that vocation that is meaningful to you You make a great point. I can see why it does look like that from the outside. But the way I see it, these people don't necessarily hate their job, they just have other things they would prefer to do than work ~40 hours a week. I enjoy my job, but I would much rather spend my short time here with my wife and child (when he arrives in December). Financial freedom will allow me to do that. Although I wouldn't fully retire, I would cut down to part time, or find more meaningful work to keep me busy a couple days a week.
As for living like a monk, that's where the reorganising of priorities comes in. Some people go frugal to the extreme, and others spend everything they earn – I like to be somewhere in the middle. Saving for the future but still enjoying life now, we go out to dinner with friends 1-2 times per week etc, but I make a conscious effort to not overspend on unnecessary things, and also to save costs where I can (like insurance etc)
[User #1172355657 postsElseWhirlpool Forums Addict] I started thinking about this in my early 40s. Concluded that I wanted the flexibility to stop working in a traditional job at the time of my choosing – but certainly before the traditional retirement age. This requires a good super balance, as well as a decent chunk of investible funds outside super. I've never lived like a monk (other than as a child of poor parents). But having a good job in the right industry helps. Managing spending also helps – expensive sports cars were tempting, but I managed to resist.
I reached Financial Independence at 50. Continued to work for a few years in a large company – reduced hours, doing stuff I like. Eventually called it quits – the meaningful part of the job was eroded by the busywork that happens in most companies. If the old days I would just suck it up and keep working. But once you achieve financial independence, your mindset changes – you don't have to endure this stuff if you don't want to.
Tips: do a plan, spend less than you earn, become financially literate, invest, aim to get rich slowly. Boring, but effective.
Also think about what you'd do if you stop working. For many people this is the hard bit. I know plenty of people with significant wealth who are afraid to stop working.

I am interested in hearing peoples reasons for doing this in the first place.
There is more to life than working?
From a very high-level it looks like people are working hard in jobs they don't particularly like – living like monks – and saving like mad. Then at some point they will be able to stop working – live off their assets – and then what?
Some people love working, and that is great. Others have figured that with their one shot at life, why spend it working if you don't have to. So for a few years of saving and delayed gratification, you can have your expenses paid for – forever – by income producing assets.
Then you can do whatever you like – travelling, playing video games all day, whatever – without the need to work.
Of course, some people prefer the "FI" part (Financial Independence) only and will still go to work, however it seems those people are much happier than the typical employee because they don't have to be there if they don't want to. If there is too much BS at work then they can leave.
Of course, people that have no hobbies or other interests outside of work will unlikely see the point of FIRE.

Cory the Creator writes...
I'm keen to see if anyone has walked the path and has tips or insight
I'd suggest some reading material -
The Millionaire Next Door (Thomas J. Stanley and William D. Danko)
Stop Acting Rich (Thomas J. Stanley)
Your Money or Your Life (Vicki Robin)
The basic message is that people work to accumulate "stuff" and much of the time it is for status reasons (new phone, new car, bigger house, or whatever). The media has done an amazing job to convince people that if they buy this stuff they will be happy, or that they can emulate a wealthy celebrity by purchasing the same things.
It is almost a reflex to see a big house, or someone driving an expensive car, and think "Wow! They must be rich!". Statistics show this mostly isn't true. There is typically a lot of debt behind those items, however humans tend to take first impressions and not consider the reality.
So to be truly on the FIRE path, you need to be aware of this. Be mindful of advertising and consumption. Be aware of the dollar cost of time – such as "if you are paid $100/day and you buy a new $500 phone, is that phone really worth five whole days of work?".
There are wealthy people everywhere, and you wouldn't pick them in the crowd because they don't look wealthy. To reach FIRE, you will become wealthy, however the habits that made you wealthy will stick and you won't actually care about how you are "supposed" to look or behave as a (so called) wealthy person would.
Some call this "stealth wealth".
You'll also come across the 4% rule. Essentially, you can withdraw 4% of your portfolio each year for living expenses forever and there is a high chance (97%?) you'll never touch the principal. If you reduce to withdrawing 3.5% or so, you are guaranteed to never run out of money. Very likely your portfolio will grow as well.
So you work backwards to see how much you need. For example, if you can live on $40,000/year then you need 25x that amount – $1,000,000 in income producing assets (shares etc) – i.e. 4% of $1M is $40,000.
FIRE is all based on simple math. Based on 4%, if you had a monthly expense of $20 for the phone (or whatever) you would need 300 x $20 = $6000 invested to pay for that monthly expense forever. The 300 comes from 12 months in a year multiplied by 25.
Keeping this in mind might also change your perception of value. For example, $20/month for a magazine subscription really needs $6000 invested – is the magazine worth it?
One way of visualising this is to plot your savings against a calendar. When every day of the year is "paid for", you have reached FIRE -
https://engaging-data.com/freedom-calculator
Savings rate is extremely important. It is great you are starting at age 25 – you have heaps of time. Put some numbers into a calculator such as this -
https://networthify.com/calculator/earlyretirement
If you can save 50% of your income and invest it, you will retire in about 16 years (early 40's for you!). If you save 75% you'll retire in about 7 years. These numbers assume no existing investments. Pick a comfortable savings rate and try to stick with it.

When FI is attained, hopefully one is still young, energetic and into their prime. He/she can either work for the pleasure, knowing that there is a passive income. Whatever earn from that point onward is either play money or build up a further level of security. By all means travel/enjoy/live it up after FI.
To live like a pensioner, counting pennies and not productive whilst still able body is not my cup of tea.

I'm 54, I class myself as FI rather than FIRE, have achieved FI about 5 years ago. I've remained working full time as I really enjoy my job, FI gives me options, I go to work because I choose to, and not because I have to. Being able to determine your own destiny, make your own choices without having to be a slave to any job or anyone, that's what I've strived for. I've targeting retiring next year, but who knows, if I continue to feel enjoyment at work, I'll stay on, just maybe reduce my hours.
